title: Indian Muslims: Who Are They
lede: K.S. Lal, a historian of the Delhi Sultanate, reconstructs how India's Muslim population grew, using chronicles, travellers' accounts and early censuses. His answer to the title's question: most Indian Muslims descend from Hindus who converted, mostly under pressure. A small minority descend from immigrant Turks, Persians, Arabs and Afghans. His second question is why, unlike Persia, Iraq or Egypt, India was never fully converted.
facts: Muslims as a share of India's population around 1400, about 3 million, by Lal's estimate
Muslims in 1600, out of about 140 million
in 1800: about 25 million out of 170 million
the Muslim–Hindu ratio by 1900, against about 1:7 in 1800
note: Population figures for medieval India are estimates. Lal's are his own and contested: other historians give different numbers and weigh conversion by force, Sufi influence and social mobility differently. This page reports his estimates and reasoning as his.

sections.title: Muslims as a share of India's people
sections.lede: Lal's figures for the Muslim share of the population in what is now India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. He notes that the total population rose and fell over the medieval period while the Muslim population “shows only a constant rise”.
items: About 3 million (“more than thirty lakh”), under 2%
About 15 million of 140 million, “one-ninth to one-tenth”
About 25 million of 170 million, a ratio of about 1:7 to Hindus
A 1:6 ratio, per Bishop Heber (1826) and Thornton's Gazetteer (1854)
A 1:5 ratio
sections.note: Values come from the figures and ratios Lal gives. For the ratio years, the percentage is the nearest he states or implies.

rows: On the invasion route for a thousand years, with heavy immigration.
After Shah Mir arrived from Swat in 1315 and his dynasty took power.
A dynasty descended from a converted Rajput. Ahmad Shah's strict jizya from 1414.
Jalaluddin, the converted son of Raja Ganesh. The historian Wise thought more converts were made then than in the next 300 years. Sufis played a part.
Bahmani wars with Vijayanagara brought captives who became Muslims, along with foreign nobles.
Trade and pearl fisheries. The Portuguese put Muslims at about 20%.
Stayed largely Hindu: the imperial heartland was not enemy country, and Rajputana was never held.

sections.title: What drove growth, and what checked it

items: Conversion, “mainly”: war captives, state policy, jizya, rewards, Sufi preaching
Immigration of soldiers, scholars and adventurers
Polygamy and mixed marriages, whose children were raised Muslim
Higher fertility, as in every census from 1881 to 1941 according to Kingsley Davis
Fewer war losses, since Hindu foot soldiers bore the brunt
The country's size: no ruler ever held all of India
A Hindu “Protestant” movement: bhakti saints and resistance to conversion
Caste, which Lal says worked as a “bulwark” more than a push to convert
Akbar's 1562 ban on enslaving war captives
Portuguese missions competing from 1498
Muslim infighting: six of ten Slave-dynasty sultans deposed or murdered

sections.q: The sword of Islam was blunted in India.
